policies.summary: Counties may adopt standards for commercial wind and solar facilities but none more restrictive than the statute, may not ban them (even temporarily) in agricultural or industrial districts, must approve compliant applications, and may not set stricter sound, height, decommissioning or property-value conditions. The law exempts projects filed before 2023-01-27, an industrial enterprise zone near the I-88/I-39 interchange (Lee-Ogle, added by P.A. 103-81) and an area in Madison County (added by P.A. 104-458).

From 2026-06-01, counties with zoning may regulate stand-alone energy storage systems only within limits set by statute: no requirements stricter than the statute or NFPA 855, no stricter sound limits than the Pollution Control Board rules, and compliant applications must be approved.

A developer of a wind, solar or storage facility of 50 MW or more in an unincorporated area may petition the Illinois Commerce Commission when a local government violates the state siting law; the Commission may issue a siting certificate if the local government denied the project, missed the statutory deadline, or never adopted a compliant ordinance, and the certificate authorizes construction.

Counties grant siting approval or special use permits for commercial wind, solar and (from 2026-06-01) energy storage facilities under state-set limits; the state has no permitting authority of its own. Since 2026-06-01 the Illinois Commerce Commission may issue a siting certificate for a facility of 50 MW or more in unincorporated areas if a local government denies or fails to act in violation of the state siting law (see IL-local_preemption-3).

Statute sets the maximum setbacks a county may require: for wind towers 2.1 times blade-tip height from nonparticipating homes and community buildings and 1.1 times from nonparticipating property lines and roads, plus a 30-hour yearly shadow-flicker limit; for solar 150 feet from nonparticipating homes and 50 feet from property lines and roads, fencing of 6 to 25 feet, and panels no taller than 20 feet. Sound limits may be no stricter than state Pollution Control Board rules.

Counties regulating stand-alone energy storage must require setbacks of 150 feet from occupied community buildings and nonparticipating homes, 50 feet from their property lines and from road rights-of-way, and perimeter fencing of 7 to 25 feet; nonparticipating owners may waive the setbacks.

projects.description: On February 3, 2023, the Piatt County Zoning Board of Appeals voted against recommending a zoning permit for Apex Clean Energy’s 300-MW, 50-turbine Goose Creek wind project.
In 2015, Clean Line Energy proposed a project to build 207 miles of a high-voltage direct current (HVDC) power line between the Mississippi River and Indiana border to transmit clean energy.
In June 2018, residents of Newman Township voted 86-57 in favor of enacting a zoning ordinance to block the proposed 200-MW Harvest Ridge Wind Farm.

Considerable opposition to the construction of a 7,600-acre, 200-MW wind farm in the Mount Pulaski area led the Logan County board to initially deny the application for a conditional use permit in 2015.

On August 14, 2024, the Rockford City Council voted unanimously to oppose a 5-MW solar farm that would be located on 32 acres of farmland, although city officials expressed doubt that they have the authority to stop the project under state law.

In April 2020, the Logan County Planning and Zoning Commission voted 4-2 to table the conditional use permit applications for up to 82 wind turbines after a group called Concerned Citizens for a Safe Logan County expressed concerns regarding population density, sound levels and environmental protection.
In 2014, Invenergy LLC applied to build a 136-turbine, 250-MW wind energy project in Livingston County, which faced opposition from a local group called United Citizens for Livingston County.
In January 2023, the Princeton City Council voted to table a resolution to allow for the construction of a 7-acre solar array in the city’s Technology Park.
In February 2023, the Tazewell County Board unanimously rejected a zoning change that would have allowed SolarStone Partners to establish a solar farm near Illinois Central Christian School.
As of November 2022, over 1,000 people had signed a petition opposing plans for the 200-MW, 60-turbine Top Hat Wind Project over concerns about interference with radar.
